strengths: Well-motivated problem identifying clear limitations of existing VLM-based approaches for progress estimation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple distribution shifts (environment, embodiment, task) with detailed ablations on temporal memory strategies
Consistent and substantial improvements over GVL baselines across most test scenarios (e.g., 0.78 vs 0.25 VOC on in-distribution)
Technically sound approach combining meta-learning, test-time training, and self-supervised learning in a coherent framework
Good experimental design with multiple shift types and clear presentation of method pipeline
weaknesses: Limited novelty: straightforward combination of existing techniques (meta-learning from Finn et al. 2017, test-time training from Sun et al. 2020) without substantial innovation
Narrow evaluation scope: single simulated dataset (BridgeData V2) only, no real-world robot experiments, no validation of whether improved VOC translates to downstream task performance
Unfair comparison with main baseline: GVL uses Gemini 1.5 Pro (different model/training data) while this method trains on BridgeData; unclear which component drives improvements
Confounded design choices: TTT-IM vs TTT-EX differ in both parameter retention AND context window size (k=0 vs k=7), making it unclear which drives improvements
Insufficient technical details: self-supervised loss definition sparse, meta-learning gradient computation not clearly described, no analysis of computational cost or inference overhead
Missing critical ablations: no comparison with supervised test-time fine-tuning, no ablation on dissimilarity-based sampling, hyperparameter sensitivity unexplored (single tep=1 step)
Lack of statistical rigor: no error bars/confidence intervals, small test sets (200 samples), no multiple runs across random seeds, no significance tests
No failure analysis: ms_sweep underperforms (0.49 VOC) with no explanation; no qualitative examples, error modes, or visualization of adapted representations
Reproducibility concerns: code not mentioned as available, validation set composition unclear, some hyperparameter selection details missing
Metric limitations: VOC only measures temporal ordering correlation, not absolute progress prediction accuracy; doesn't assess whether metric improvements help actual RL/task performance

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation across multiple distribution shifts (environment, embodiment, task) with 10 datasets from BridgeData V2
Clear problem motivation addressing temporal shortcuts in progress estimation with a principled approach
Consistent improvements over GVL baselines (Table 1) across diverse settings
Useful ablation studies comparing trajectory-level vs. step-by-step adaptation showing benefits of implicit memory
Good presentation with clear figures (Figure 1) and detailed appendices with hyperparameter specifications
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is primarily a straightforward combination of existing techniques (TTT, meta-learning, self-supervised learning) without substantial innovation beyond simple dissimilarity-based sampling

Unclear what the model actually learns: no evidence that improvements come from capturing temporal context vs. simply overfitting to test trajectories; continuous parameter updates at test-time are essentially online fitting to individual test sets

Unfair baseline comparison: GVL is trained on diverse web data without task supervision while the proposed method uses domain-specific expert demonstrations; VLM's zero-shot approach is more practical despite lower scores
Self-supervised objective poorly motivated: the reconstruction loss and its connection to reducing temporal bias are unclear, lacking formal justification or visualization of learned representations

Narrow training distribution: trained only on pick-and-place with WidowX250 in ToyKitchen (2,986 demos), with folding/sweeping/stacking only in evaluation; claims of 'generalization from single training environment' are overstated
No statistical rigor: missing confidence intervals, significance tests, or error analysis; small test sets (100-200 trajectories) without variance estimates

Critical missing analyses: no robustness testing across trajectory lengths, no ablation on dissimilarity sampling vs. alternatives, no computational cost analysis, no per-trajectory generalization evaluation
Hyperparameter choices under-justified: λ_self=0.5, w_train=8, b=8, learning rate η=0.1 appear arbitrary; hyperparameters tuned on validation set risks overfitting
Incomplete baseline comparisons: missing comparisons with other meta-learning methods, test-time adaptation variants, and simple fine-tuning baselines
Reproducibility concerns: no mention of code release, self-supervised loss never formally defined, key implementation details missing (exact GVL prompts, sensitivity analyses)

strengths: Strong empirical results with substantial improvements over state-of-the-art in-context learning (GVL), achieving 3x better VOC in many cases
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple distribution shifts (environment, embodiment, task) with systematic dataset design
Well-motivated problem addressing real limitations of existing approaches for progress estimation in robotic manipulation
Clear methodology combining meta-learning with test-time adaptation and thoughtful dissimilarity-based sampling to encourage semantic understanding
Thorough ablation studies (Table 3) demonstrating the value of implicit memory over trajectory-level or reset-based adaptation
Good reproducibility with detailed architectural specs, hyperparameters, and training procedures in appendices
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty - primarily applies existing techniques (Sun et al. 2020 test-time training, Finn et al. 2017 meta-learning) to a new domain without significant innovation

Insufficient explanation of the critical self-supervised loss component: projection matrices P_V, P_K, P_Q introduced with minimal justification; learning procedure and reconstruction objective structure not clearly specified

Narrow experimental scope: training limited to 2,986 demonstrations from single robot in ToyKitchen; all evaluations remain within similar robotic manipulation settings; claims of 'generalizable task progress estimation' overstated

Unfair baseline comparison: GVL not designed for progress estimation; no ablation showing impact of fine-tuning GVL on this task; critical missing computational cost analysis comparing test-time adaptation overhead vs. GVL inference

Scalability concerns unaddressed: method requires full trajectory access at inference time; applicability to online/streaming settings unclear; computational complexity with trajectory length not analyzed

Incomplete analysis: no error analysis or discussion of failure cases (e.g., ms_sweep VOC of 0.4898 vs. 0.6-0.8 for others); no visualization of learned representations; missing sensitivity analysis on hyperparameters like window size k

Technical clarity issues: meta-learning procedure underspecified (gradient backpropagation through adaptation steps?); fundamental tension between assuming monotonic progress (t/T) and stated goal of mitigating temporal bias
Evaluation limitations: VOC metric measures chronological order alignment but may not suit all tasks; no justification for metric choice or exploration of alternatives

strengths: Clear problem motivation identifying genuine limitations of existing VLM-based value function approaches (temporal modeling vs. monotonic bias)
Sound technical approach applying meta-learned test-time training to value function learning with principled design
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple distribution shifts (environment, task, embodiment) with thorough ablations
Strong and consistent empirical results: outperforms GVL on VOC metrics (0.6-0.82 vs 0.15-0.4), achieves perfect discrimination (BinVOC=1.0), and exceeds Meta-World dense rewards
Well-executed experimental methodology with proper statistical analysis (stratified bootstrap CI, multiple seeds), reproducible code details, and open-source models
Novel combination of sequential parameter updates for implicit temporal memory encoding, empirically validated to outperform trajectory-level and non-temporal adaptation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core components (test-time training, meta-learned self-supervised losses) from Sun et al. [34]; main contribution is application to value functions with dissimilarity sampling
Narrow evaluation scope restricted to robotic manipulation with short-horizon tasks; no evaluation on longer horizons, other domains, or tasks violating monotonic progress assumption
Incomplete main baseline comparison: cannot directly evaluate against GVL on Meta-World MT10 due to Gemini API costs; claim about folding bias is speculative and unsupported
Method assumes monotonically increasing task progress (V(o_t;g)=t/T), severely limiting applicability to tasks with non-monotonic progress, yet this critical limitation receives minimal discussion

Insufficient analysis of what TTA learns: no visualization of parameter evolution θ_t, no mechanistic understanding of semantic vs. temporal feature capture, mechanism of 'history encoding' remains opaque

Dissimilarity-based sampling lacks rigor: heuristic approximation (Eq. 5) to NP-hard problem (Eq. 4) has unknown approximation quality; authors acknowledge only 'empirical evidence' with theoretical analysis deferred
Practical safety concerns in deployment (updating value function at every timestep) insufficiently addressed and relegated to limitations without proposed mitigations
Hyperparameter sensitivity under-explored: many hyperparameters (λ_self, w_tr, k, η, t_ep) with limited sensitivity analysis; selections appear somewhat ad-hoc
Evaluation metrics limitations: VOC captures only ranking (insensitive to magnitude errors); BinVOC is coarse-grained; no analysis of absolute prediction quality
Training data scope limited to 2,986 pick-and-place demos; generalization to other task categories only demonstrated on related short-horizon tasks

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple distribution shifts (task, environment, embodiment) with consistent improvements over baselines
Well-motivated identification of limitations in existing VLM-based value functions (lack of temporal modeling in contrastive VLMs, monotonic bias in autoregressive VLMs)
Practical method that adapts frozen CLIP representations without requiring large-scale retraining, with reasonable computational overhead
Solid ablation studies demonstrating benefits of dissimilarity-based sampling and step-by-step temporal adaptation
Strong and consistent VOC improvements across multiple datasets (e.g., 0.782 vs 0.269 for GVL-0S on in-distribution data)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (test-time training from prior work [34,39] and standard gradient-based meta-learning [35]) without significant conceptual advancement

Problematic baseline comparisons: (1) GVL comparison uses Gemini 1.5 Pro without justification while acknowledging comparison is infeasible at scale on Meta-World; (2) paper reports Qwen-VL and GPT-4o 'failed' suggesting cherry-picking; (3) CLIP-FT given 8× larger projection and 10× more training steps

Evaluation metric limitations: VOC only measures monotonic correlation with time, not actual task progress—trajectories that are monotonically increasing but absolutely wrong achieve high VOC; BinVOC is binary and cannot distinguish performance levels

Temporal reasoning claims overstated: single gradient step on small adaptation module (d'=64) cannot capture rich temporal semantics; learning rate η=0.1 not justified; mechanism for how one step provides significant improvements unexplained
Strong unvalidated assumption: assumes V_πE(o_t; g) = t/T holds for expert trajectories; many tasks violate this (non-linear progress, repetitive motions); no analysis of when assumption breaks down

Limited experimental scope: only robotic manipulation with similar visual characteristics (all BridgeData V2); training and evaluation on same domain with similar visual/structural properties; no evaluation on other domains; ms_sweep consistently underperforms with no analysis of failure modes

Weak justification for dissimilarity-based sampling: authors acknowledge 'theoretical analysis of how diversity-based sampling influences shortcut learning remains a promising direction' indicating they don't understand their own mechanism; scripted datasets generated by randomized controller, not truly suboptimal demonstrations

Critical design choices lack justification: why is single gradient step sufficient? Why learning rate 0.1 specifically? Why projection dimension d'=64? Most choices selected via 'validation performance' without principled reasoning

Reproducibility concerns: BridgeData V2 not fully public; many hyperparameter selections unexplained; computational cost of test-time gradient steps not discussed; no ablation on whether simpler alternatives (random projections, frozen adaptation) work similarly

Incomplete analysis of key claims: no visualization of temporal information captured by adaptation; no analysis of how method handles trajectory phases (beginning vs. end); sensitivity to trajectory length not studied; mechanism explaining why reconstruction loss improves value prediction not provided

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear articulation of limitations in prior approaches (contrastive VLMs lack temporal reasoning; autoregressive VLMs inherit monotonic bias)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple distribution shift axes (environment, embodiment, task), proper baselines including SOTA, meaningful ablations, and downstream application to offline RL

Strong and consistent empirical results: VITA achieves 0.6-0.82 VOC across all settings vs. 0.15-0.4 for baselines; perfect expert/non-expert discrimination (BinVOC=1.0); outperforms Meta-World fuzzy rewards (0.815 vs 0.779 IQM)

Solid technical execution: elegant use of sequential parameter updates to implicitly encode trajectory history; meta-learned self-supervised loss design is principled; dissimilarity-based sampling effectively mitigates shortcut learning (Table 4)
Good reproducibility: clear architectural details, comprehensive hyperparameter specifications, training procedures documented, datasets from public source, proper evaluation protocols
Effective ablation studies validating design choices (Tables 4-5, Appendices F.1-F.2 show benefits of incremental vs. trajectory-level updates and importance of diversity-based sampling)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing techniques (test-time training from Sun et al. 2020 + standard MAML-style meta-learning) to value function learning; while the combination is novel, each component is well-established, making the core contribution somewhat incremental

Critical missing comparison: GVL results unavailable on Meta-World MT10 (offline RL task where practical benefits should be most evident) due to Gemini inference cost and open-source alternatives yielding unreliable estimates; this significantly weakens claims about SOTA performance for reward shaping

Limited failure analysis: method struggles on long-horizon tasks (ms_sweep: 0.490 vs 0.6-0.82 on others) with minimal investigation; Section 6 mentions challenges with 'high execution variability or extended durations' but provides no experimental analysis; generalization claims limited to robotic manipulation

Practical applicability concerns: updating value function at every timestep is flagged as 'potentially unsafe during deployment' but dismissed without analysis; unclear how robust method is to mid-trajectory distribution shifts or adversarial perturbations; limits real-world deployment

Dissimilarity-based sampling lacks theoretical grounding: connection to shortcut learning prevention is empirically validated but not deeply justified; authors acknowledge missing 'theoretical analysis' of how diversity-based sampling influences shortcut learning; no comparison to other diversity metrics

Insufficient hyperparameter sensitivity analysis: sweeps only learning rates and adaptation steps (Appendix D.2); no robustness analysis for other hyperparameters (w_tr, k, s, d'); unclear if design choices (e.g., t_ep=1 vs. multiple steps) are optimal across problem settings

VOC metric limitations not addressed: VOC measures rank correlation only, insensitive to absolute prediction accuracy; a constant-percentile predictor could achieve high VOC but be useless; paper lacks analysis of actual value prediction magnitudes or absolute errors relative to true progress

Limited temporal reasoning analysis: despite claims of addressing temporal context, provides no visualization of learned temporal patterns, no mechanistic analysis of what the adaptation module learns, no comparison to simpler temporal models (RNNs, Transformers)

Incomplete ablations: no isolated analysis of meta-learning contribution vs. self-supervised loss; no ablation of individual projections (P_K, P_V, P_Q); self-supervised loss (Eq. 1) design not justified—why L2 reconstruction over alternatives? No exploration of different adaptation architectures

Framing concerns: claims 'single training environment' but trains on 4 configurations of same environment; 'zero-shot' is misleading since method requires training with temporal progress labels; evaluation scope limited to robotic manipulation without domain generalization analysis
